query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporate a small reactive element addition of yttrium (approximately 1–2 wt.%) into the Si-20Cr-20Fe slurry coating to promote the in‐situ formation of a finely dispersed, adherent yttrium-enriched oxide at the outer surface, thereby enhancing high-temperature oxygen resistance of MoNbTaTiW RHEA.
generation.material_initial_state: MoNbTaTiW RHEA coated with the conventional fused slurry Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating that forms a double-layer structure (outer MSi2 and inner M5Si3) as reported in PMC7475834.
generation.intervention: Modify the slurry formulation by adding 1–2 wt.% yttrium to the Si-20Cr-20Fe mixture prior to coating deposition and thermal treatment.
generation.conditions: Static air oxidation at 1300 °C for 1 hour, which is within the extreme-temperature regime for RHEAs used in structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The yttrium is expected to segregate to the oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation, promoting the formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent yttrium-enriched oxide (likely a modified silicate or mixed oxide scale).
generation.mechanism: Reactive element effects (REE) such as those known from superalloy technology enhance oxide adhesion and reduce the growth rate and spallation of oxide scales. Yttrium segregates to the oxide grain boundaries and interfaces, reducing defect density and retarding oxygen diffusion into the underlying silicide and substrate layers. This should mitigate the rapid oxidation linked to silicon diffusion observed in the baseline coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxide scale growth (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide layers) compared to the untreated Si-20Cr-20Fe coating, potentially achieving a 30–50% improvement in oxidation resistance. The improvement is expected in the specified regime, though the exact quantitative effect has some uncertainty.
generation.baseline: The conventional Si-20Cr-20Fe coating on MoNbTaTiW RHEA, which shows multilayer oxide/silicide formation with cracks and extensive silicon diffusion upon oxidation at 1300 °C.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is expected under static air conditions at around 1300 °C for exposures on the order of 1 hour; performance under dynamic or longer exposure conditions remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The precise segregation behavior of yttrium in the complex multicomponent silicide system is uncertain; pilot experiments or thermodynamic simulations would be needed to optimize the Y content without disrupting the silicide structure.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M5Si3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. verdicts.intervention: Apply a controlled surface pre-alloying (or similar surface modification) to enrich the near‐surface region in aluminum prior to high-temperature exposure.
verdicts.fix: Clarify and optimize the pre‑alloying treatment parameters to ensure that the increased surface Al not only diffuses sufficiently but also overcomes the kinetics that normally favor CrTaO₄ formation.

paper_did: Examined the oxidation behavior of a novel NV1 refractory high-entropy alloy (containing Al, Cr, Mo, Nb, Si, Ta, Ti) with a heterogeneous microstructure (Mo‐rich dendrites with Cr-/Al‐rich interdendritic regions) by subjecting it to long‐term (up to 200 hours) isothermal oxidation tests at 1000 °C and 1100 °C in flowing dry air.

Conducted thermogravimetric analyses (TGA) and isothermal furnace exposures coupled with detailed microstructural characterizations (XRD, SEM, EDS, TEM) to identify the phases and morphologies of the oxidation scales and internal oxidation/nitridation zones.

Evaluated the influence of kinetic factors on oxide scale formation; specifically, at 1000 °C a porous CrTaO₄‐based oxide predominated (leading to an exponential oxidation weight gain) and at 1100 °C a denser CrTaO₄‐based scale formed (yielding a three‐stage, parabolic oxidation behavior).
paper_reported: At 1000 °C, NV1 exhibited an exponential mass gain (6.53 mg/cm² after 200 hours) due to the inability to form a dense protective oxide, with the external scale mainly comprising porous CrTaO₄-based oxide along with dispersed Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃.

At 1100 °C, the oxidation mass gain was lower (4.03 mg/cm² after 200 hours) and displayed three distinct stages, attributed to the formation of a denser and more continuous CrTaO₄-based oxide layer that acted as a partial diffusion barrier.

Detailed analyses revealed that the as-cast alloy’s microstructure (Mo-rich dendrites; Cr-/Al-rich interdendritic regions) led to heterogeneous oxidation, and that both oxidation and nitridation (e.g., formation of TiN) contributed to the overall weight gain.
paper_proposed: Future investigations should focus on examining the nature, adhesion, and growth mechanisms of the CrTaO₄-based oxide to further improve long-term oxidation resistance.

The role of minor alloying additions—such as Si for nitridation resistance—and their effects on the kinetics of external scale formation are suggested as important directions for enhancing oxidation performance.

Extending oxidation tests to longer durations and exploring processing modifications (beyond simple compositional changes) are proposed to better understand and optimize the protective oxide scale formation in RHEAs.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Enhancing the surface Al concentration via a pre-alloying treatment will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, dense Al₂O₃ layer that retards oxygen ingress and improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An NV1-type refractory high-entropy alloy with a heterogeneous microstructure (Mo-rich dendrites and Cr-/Al-rich interdendritic regions) as described in PMC6513993, where the dominant external oxide is porous CrTaO₄ accompanied by dispersed Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled surface pre-alloying (or similar surface modification) to enrich the near‐surface region in aluminum prior to high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose treated samples in flowing dry air at 1100 °C for 200 hours; these conditions are selected because the paper shows that at 1100 °C a denser oxide scale forms compared to 1000 °C.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent, and dense Al₂O₃ scale formed on the treated surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: By increasing the local Al concentration at the surface, the kinetics for Al diffusion and its oxidation are enhanced. This accelerates the formation of an Al₂O₃ layer, which, due to its low oxygen permeability and high thermodynamic stability, serves as an effective barrier against further oxygen ingress. This contrasts with the porous CrTaO₄-based oxide normally forming in the untreated alloy (PMC6513993::web::009, PMC6513993::web::012).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in oxidation mass gain (potentially on the order of 30–50% lower than the untreated alloy’s ~4 mg/cm² gain over 200 hours) and the formation of a more uniform and continuous oxide scale.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated NV1 alloy which shows a 4.03 mg/cm² mass gain at 1100 °C over 200 hours with a predominantly porous CrTaO₄-based scale.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is expected to work at temperatures where Al₂O₃ formation is kinetically accessible (e.g., near or at 1100 °C in dry air); if the Al availability or its oxidation kinetics are insufficient, the protective layer may not form.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement is uncertain due to potential complexities in multi-element diffusion and competitive oxide formation.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: A modified oxide scale—either an improved CrTaO₄-based layer or a composite oxide—that incorporates yttrium at the metal/oxide interface to reduce defects and enhance adhesion.
hypotheses.mechanism: Reactive elements like Y are known (e.g., in high-temperature stainless steels and thermal barrier coatings as noted in TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028) to segregate to the oxide scale grain boundaries. This ‘reactive element effect’ reduces the growth of defects and voids at the oxide/metal interface, effectively slowing oxygen diffusion. hypotheses.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxidation mass gain relative to the untreated alloy (expected improvement could be on the order of >25% reduction in mass gain) and observable improvements in the coherence and density of the oxide layer.

The effect should be observable under high-temperature oxidizing conditions but might be less pronounced at lower temperatures where oxide kinetics differ.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude of improvement is subject to the complex interplay of multi-element oxidation and scale formation; precise values are not well established.

paper_did: Prepared MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloy substrates via spark plasma sintering and applied a Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating using a fused slurry method.
Conducted high‐temperature oxidation tests in air at 1000 °C and 1300 °C for 1 hour under static conditions.
Characterized the coatings with X‐ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and energy dispersive spectroscopy to analyze phase compositions, microstructures, and elemental gradients.

Identified that the as-prepared coating exhibits a double-layer structure—with an outer high-silicon disilicide (MSi2) layer and an inner low-silicon silicide (M5Si3) layer—and observed significant silicon diffusion into the substrate during oxidation.
paper_reported: The initial silicide coating shows a distinct two-layer structure; the outer layer consists mainly of disilicide (MSi2) with ~66.7% Si, while the inner layer is mainly M5Si3 with ~37.5% Si.

During oxidation, silicon diffuses from the coating into the RHEA substrate and the oxidation process produces an outer oxide layer whose structure (including layer number, thickness, and defect features) depends on the oxidation temperature.

At 1000 °C a three-layer system (two silicide layers and one oxide layer, with gaps and cracks due to volume expansion) is observed, and at 1300 °C a more complex four-layer structure develops with a thicker, more complete oxide scale.
paper_proposed: The study demonstrates that the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating can protect RHEAs from high-temperature oxidation by forming a multi-layered silicide/oxide structure, implying that further investigation into coating modifications or alternative compositions may further optimize oxidation protection.

hypotheses.mechanism: Al2O3 is renowned for its dense, low-oxygen permeability, and slow-growing characteristics compared with mixed metal oxides. Incorporation of aluminum promotes the formation of this passivating layer, which acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress. This helps to suppress further oxidation of the underlying silicide layers and the RHEA substrate. By adjusting the coating’s composition, the aluminum drives a change from a heterogeneous oxide scale (as seen in the pure Si-20Cr-20Fe coating) to a more protective alumina-dominated scale.

hypotheses.uncertainty: While alumina formation generally enhances protection, the optimal aluminum content and its influence on coating adhesion and mechanical properties require further experimental validation.

paper_did: Synthesized an equimolar MoNbTaTiW refractory high‐entropy alloy via spark plasma sintering from high‐purity elemental powders.

Performed oxidation tests on cube samples (5×5×5 mm) in a static air atmosphere at two temperatures (1000 °C and 1300 °C) for 1 hour with a controlled heating rate.
paper_reported: The initial coating exhibited a double‐layer silicide structure: an outer, high-silicon layer identified as disilicide (MSi2) and an inner, lower-silicon layer identified as M5Si3.

During high-temperature oxidation, silicon diffused from the coating into the RHEA substrate, causing the silicide layer to move inward and increase in thickness, while the coating surface transformed into an oxide layer whose structure (e.g., single vs. double oxide layers, presence of bulges and cracks) depended strongly on the oxidation temperature.

Detailed microstructural evolution was characterized via XRD, SEM, EDS, and schematically represented as layered structures (L1: M5Si3; L2: MSi2; L3 and L4: complex oxide layers) that changed with oxidation conditions.
paper_proposed: While the paper does not list explicit future work items, it implies that the developed Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating strategy is a promising approach for protecting RHEAs in high-temperature oxidation environments and that further optimization (for example, in controlling oxide scale morphology and diffusion behavior) would be beneficial.

papers.title: Fluorine Effect for Improving Oxidation Resistance of Ti-45Al-8.5Nb Alloy at 1000 °C.

verdicts.intervention: Spray-coating the alloy surface with a 0.15 mol/L NaF aqueous solution prior to high-temperature exposure.
verdicts.fix: Clarify and support the assumption that the specific reactivity of aluminum in the HEA matrix will enable similar volatile fluoride formation and selective oxidation by including preliminary thermodynamic or kinetic data for the chosen HEA composition.

verdicts.fix: Include a preliminary thermodynamic and kinetic analysis of the AlF₃-to-Al₂O₃ conversion reaction under the targeted oxidation conditions, and consider small-scale experiments to verify that a thin AlF₃ coating indeed converts fully to a protective, adherent α-Al₂O₃ layer on HEAs.

verdicts.fix: Provide more detailed process parameters and a mechanistic rationale—such as supporting thermodynamic calculations and consideration of competing fluoride formations for non-Al elements—to ensure that gas-phase fluorination will selectively promote Al₂O₃ formation without deleterious side reactions.

paper_did: Prepared Ti-45Al-8.5Nb (γ‐TiAl based) alloy specimens by casting, cutting, grinding, and polishing.
Applied a surface treatment by spraying a 0.15 mol/L NaF-containing aqueous solution onto the alloy, including on specimens with artificially induced microcracks.
Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments at 1000 °C (for durations of 2 h and 100 h) in a tube furnace, ensuring controlled conditions.
Characterized the treated and oxidized specimens using SEM, EDS, XRD, TEM, and contact angle measurements to assess microstructure, phase composition, and oxidation kinetics.
paper_reported: Fluorine treatment reduced the oxidation weight gain dramatically (from 6.03 mg/cm² for the bare alloy to 0.81 mg/cm² for the fluorine‐treated alloy).
The treatment promoted the formation of an outer protective Al₂O₃ scale with excellent adhesion, while suppressing the detrimental growth of TiO₂ in most regions.
In specimens with artificial microcracks, rapid TiO₂ growth occurred along the cracks during short-time oxidation, while a continuous, fine Al₂O₃ film developed underneath during extended oxidation.
A hierarchical oxide structure was revealed, featuring an Al₂O₃‐rich top layer, an Al‐depleted subsurface, and a Nb‐rich interface that contributes to oxygen diffusion hindrance.
paper_proposed: The paper suggests that the fluorine treatment approach can be used as a repair method for protective oxide films on components such as turbine blades and disks.
It implies that reintroduction of fluorine via a simple spraying method can extend the lifetime of γ‐TiAl alloys by regenerating protective oxide scales.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A simple surface treatment by spraying a dilute NaF-containing aqueous solution onto the refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the formation of a continuous, adherent α-Al2O3 scale that significantly improves high-temperature oxygen resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy with a microstructure containing aluminum along with refractory elements (e.g., Nb, Mo, Ta, W) in its as-cast or wrought state.
hypotheses.intervention: Spray-coating the alloy surface with a 0.15 mol/L NaF aqueous solution prior to high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at around 1000 °C (or at a temperature appropriate for the HEA composition, e.g., 900–1100 °C) for long-duration exposures (e.g., 100 h), where oxygen partial pressure is ambient.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective, continuous and dense α-Al2O3 layer that is intimately bonded to the alloy substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: Fluorine from the NaF solution reacts with reactive aluminum in the substrate to form volatile Al-fluoride species. At high temperature, these species decompose, leading to a local enrichment in Al that selectively oxidizes to form an adherent and continuous Al2O3 film. This film acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, reducing further oxidation of the refractory elements. This mechanism builds upon the fluorine effect observed in γ-TiAl alloys [PMC9030595::web::017] and leverages known benefits of Al2O3 in high-temperature oxidation resistance [TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028].
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The treated HEA should show a significant reduction (potentially an order of magnitude lower oxidation mass gain as in similar systems, although the exact value is uncertain) compared to an untreated alloy; oxide scale will be more uniform and adherent with minimal spallation.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloy oxidized under the same conditions typically develops a mixed or non-uniform oxide scale that may spall due to oxygen diffusion and differential thermal stresses.
hypotheses.boundary: This intervention is expected to work when the alloy has sufficient aluminum content to form Al2O3, and within the temperature range where the volatilization of metal fluorides and subsequent oxide formation kinetics are favorable. Extremely high temperatures or very different compositions might alter the fluorine–aluminum reaction dynamics.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., mass gain reduction) in HEAs is uncertain due to compositional differences from γ-TiAl alloys.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the NaF-treated samples do not exhibit a significantly lower oxidation mass gain, improved uniformity and adherence of an Al2O3 scale compared to untreated samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that fluorine treatment on γ-TiAl alloys promotes the formation of a protective Al2O3 film [PMC9030595::web::017]
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the fluorine surface-treatment approach from TiAl systems to refractory high-entropy alloys under extreme-temperature oxidizing conditions, testing the idea in a different alloy system with potentially different elemental interactions.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Pre-depositing a thin, conformal layer of aluminum fluoride (AlF3) onto the surface of a refractory high-entropy alloy will, upon high-temperature exposure, in situ convert to an adherent α-Al2O3 layer, thus enhancing oxygen resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy containing aluminum and other refractory elements in its standard manufactured microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Deposition of a nanometer-scale AlF3 coating through methods such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or sol–gel spin coating.
hypotheses.conditions: High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) at around 1000 °C for long durations (e.g., 100 h), under conditions relevant to structural applications.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The initial AlF3 layer that decomposes to yield an Al-enriched surface that nucleates and grows a high-quality α-Al2O3 scale.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-deposited AlF3 has a relatively high vapor pressure at elevated temperatures, and under the oxidation conditions, it decomposes and reacts with ambient oxygen to form a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale. This ceramic conversion leverages both the protective nature of Al2O3 and the controlled interface provided by an in situ–formed layer. The mechanism is analogous to the fluorine-induced selective oxidation mechanism [PMC9030595::web::004-016] but implemented via an ex situ coating that predefines the oxidation pathway.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The HEA treated with an AlF3 pre-coating should display a lower oxidation rate, with a adherent, uniform, and dense α-Al2O3 scale and a reduction in oxide spallation compared to untreated specimens. The improvement is expected to be significant though the exact improvement magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated alloys typically form non-uniform mixed oxides that offer inferior protection and may suffer spallation.
hypotheses.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective when the coating is uniform and sufficiently thin to allow complete conversion without detrimental residual fluoride phases; effectiveness may be limited on alloys with very low Al content.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantification of the conversion efficiency of AlF3 to Al2O3 and the precise reduction in oxidation rate in HEAs remains uncertain without system-specific studies.

hypotheses.what_is_new: Proposes using an ex situ AlF3 pre-coating instead of a post-treatment spraying method, targeting a controlled in situ conversion that could tailor the oxide scale’s microstructure on refractory high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Exposing refractory high-entropy alloy components to a controlled fluorine-containing gas atmosphere during heat treatment will induce in situ fluorination that promotes selective oxidation to form a durable α-Al2O3 scale, thereby enhancing high-temperature oxygen resistance.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy components in the as-processed condition with standard surface finish.
hypotheses.intervention: Heat treatment of the alloy in an oxidizing furnace atmosphere that is doped with a low partial pressure of a fluorinating gas (e.g., trace HF vapor or F2 diluted in an inert carrier).
hypotheses.conditions: Heat treatment at a high temperature such as 1000–1100 °C in an environment of air with an added controlled, low concentration of fluorine (provided via HF vapor) for durations around 100 h, under controlled pressure.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of transient metal fluorides (e.g., AlF3) on the surface, which rapidly convert to a protective α-Al2O3 layer during heat treatment.
hypotheses.mechanism: The presence of trace fluorine in the atmosphere reacts with alloy surface elements, particularly aluminum, to form volatile or transient fluorides. These species decompose or react with oxygen to yield a locally enriched Al2O3 film. The process mimics the selective oxidation pathway seen in the fluorine-treated TiAl alloys [PMC9030595::web::002-004] and is designed to occur uniformly during processing, thereby forming an adherent and dense protective oxide scale that reduces oxygen ingress.

paper_did: Employed stationary friction processing at two rotational speeds (400 and 1800 rpm for 5 min) to refine the microstructure of an as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi HEA.

Characterized the microstructural evolution via optical microscopy, EBSD, and XRD – noting ultrafine-grain sizes, phase transformations (BCC/B2 to FCC), increased strain, and compressive residual stresses.
Determined that processing increased surface free energy and promoted a high density of grain boundaries.
Performed high-temperature oxidation tests (850–1050 °C for 100 h) comparing as‐cast and processed samples.
Analyzed the oxidation kinetics and oxide scale formation (protective chromia and alumina versus non-protective spinels) via mass gain measurements, XRD, SEM, and EDS.
paper_reported: A significant reduction (12–48%) in oxidation kinetics (cumulative mass gain) for processed samples compared to the as‐cast state.

That ultrafine-grained microstructures with enhanced surface free energy and high GB density facilitate the formation of a dense, layered oxide scale (top chromia with an inner Al-rich oxide), leading to improved oxidation resistance.

Quantitative correlations between strain rate, oxide scale thickness, and activation energy for oxidation.
paper_proposed: The study suggests that microstructural tailoring (e.g., through controlled severe plastic deformation) is a promising avenue to further enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance in HEAs.
Future investigations could focus on optimizing processing parameters to control oxide scale composition and uniformity, as well as exploring other routes for protective scale formation.

hypotheses.mechanism: The Y atoms are expected to act as reactive elements that enhance the adhesion and stability of the protective Cr2O3 and Al2O3 scales by reducing oxide spallation. Their segregation at critical diffusion paths impedes oxygen ingress, leading to a lower oxidation rate. This builds upon the paper's observation that ultrafine grain structures promote protective oxide formation, while here Y doping further improves scale adherence.

hypotheses.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA subjected to the same oxidation conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected within the temperature window where protective oxides remain stable (approximately 950–1050 °C in air); outside this regime, either excessive diffusion or scale volatilization may occur.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement is uncertain due to potential interactions between Y and the complex HEA composition.

paper_did: Prepared a refractory high‐entropy alloy substrate (VZrHfNbTa) coated with metal hafnium using an embedding hot‐press sintering process at 1823 K under 30 MPa for 1 hour, followed by controlled cooling.

Utilized a carbon‐paper–separated graphite mold and electro‐deoxidation‐synthesized powders to form the coating, which resulted in in situ reactions (e.g., formation of HfC) and a graded interfacial layer.

Conducted comprehensive characterization via XRD, SEM, EDS, and energy spectrum line scans to analyze microstructure, elemental diffusion (notably zirconium diffusing ~60 μm into the coating forming an HfZr transition layer), and bonding mechanisms.

Performed high‐temperature oxidation tests in air (at approximately 1600 °C and 1873 K for 5 hours) and compared coated versus uncoated specimens by examining weight gain and changes in surface hardness.
paper_reported: The coating consists mainly of HfC with a chemically bonded, graded HfZr transition layer between the hafnium coating and the VZrHfNbTa substrate, owing to significant diffusion of zirconium.

Coated specimens exhibited much lower weight gain (56.56 mg/cm² versus 98.09 mg/cm² in uncoated samples) during oxidation and retained high surface hardness (only an ~9% drop compared to a ~57% drop in uncoated specimens).
The formation of a dense HfO₂ protective layer on the surface was identified as the key factor for the enhanced oxidation resistance and improved adhesion between the coating and the substrate.
paper_proposed: Establish an experimental foundation for high‐temperature oxidation‐resistant composite coatings on HEAs.

Suggest that further investigations into coating composition and process modifications (e.g., exploiting elemental diffusion and interface engineering) could further extend the service life of such materials in extreme environments.

paper_did: Synthesized FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high‐entropy alloy powder via gas atomization.
Deposited coatings using high‐velocity oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF) on carbon steel substrates while varying the spraying distance.
Subjected the alloy powder and coatings to multiple thermal treatments including continuous heating in air up to 1400 °C and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C.
Characterized the oxidation behavior and phase transformations using techniques such as SEM/EDX, XRD, DTA, TGA, and microhardness testing.
paper_reported: Under HVOF, in‐flight oxidation induces pronounced aluminum diffusion from the BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface, leading to surface alumina (α-Al2O3) formation and subsequent destabilization of the BCC phase (with transfer to FCC in Al-depleted regions).
Increasing the spraying distance increases oxide content and porosity, which negatively affects the microhardness despite higher alumina contents.

During continuous heating, the alloy exhibits an initial decomposition (sigma formation) of the BCC solid solution followed by aluminum diffusion to the surface and simultaneous formation of alumina and FCC phases above 800 °C.
Isothermal annealing at 800 °C shows that decomposition (with sigma formation) occurs before pronounced oxidation, with Al diffusing outward to form a thin surface oxide.
paper_proposed: Producing coatings with high alumina content by using a longer distance from the spray nozzle or a finer powder.
Using feedstock powder with an excessive aluminum concentration to mitigate unwanted FCC formation during deposition.

Employing a preliminary heat treatment of the feedstock powder to achieve a higher hardness and establish a protective alumina shell, which is beneficial for tribotechnical applications at elevated temperatures.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at an intermediate temperature can form a continuous, adherent alumina scale on the refractory high‐entropy alloy surface, thereby reducing subsequent high-temperature oxygen uptake.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a FeNiCoCrMoAl‐based alloy) with a supersaturated BCC solid solution and homogeneous composition.
hypotheses.intervention: Expose the alloy to a pre-oxidation heat treatment in air at around 800 °C for 1–3 hours prior to service.
hypotheses.conditions: Annealing in ambient air at 800 °C for a limited time (1–3 hours) to form an initial protective oxide layer; subsequent exposure during service at extreme temperatures (e.g., 1100 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, dense, and continuous α-Al2O3 (alumina) layer that adheres to the underlying alloy.
hypotheses.mechanism: The pre-formed alumina scale limits oxygen diffusion due to alumina's low oxygen permeability and high thermodynamic stability. By establishing this barrier before severe conditions are encountered, the alloy’s oxygen uptake during high-temperature service is reduced, thus improving oxidation resistance.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated alloys, the pre-oxidized alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly reduced weight gain from oxidation and better scale integrity during high-temperature exposure; the improvement might be on the order of a 30–50% reduction in oxidation rate, though the precise value is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated refractory HEA surfaces tend to oxidize rapidly under extreme temperature, with less controlled scale growth and possible spallation.
hypotheses.boundary: The pre-oxidation treatment must yield an alumina scale that remains adherent during subsequent thermal cycling and not become too thick or porous; if the scale spalls or degrades, the benefit would be lost.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Variability in scale uniformity and adhesion may result from small differences in treatment time or ambient oxygen content, and the exact improvement percentage is uncertain.

hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enrichment of aluminum at the top few microns of the alloy, facilitating the preferential formation of a uniform and continuous α-Al2O3 scale upon exposure to oxygen.
hypotheses.mechanism: The laser remelting induces rapid solidification and microsegregation, pushing Al toward the surface. A heightened surface concentration of Al will more readily react with oxygen at high temperatures to form a robust alumina layer, which serves as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated surfaces, the laser-treated alloy should exhibit a lower oxidation rate (potentially a 20–40% reduction in weight gain) under extreme-temperature conditions, although the exact improvement is somewhat uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Untreated alloys exhibit homogeneous compositions that oxidize uniformly, often leading to less adherent or discontinuous oxide layers at temperatures around 1100 °C.
hypotheses.boundary: The laser treatment parameters must be optimized to avoid damaging the surface or introducing defects; excessive remelting might cause porosity. The process is effective only if the induced Al segregation is sufficient to enhance oxide formation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The degree of Al segregation and resulting oxide layer quality depends strongly on laser process parameters, and it is uncertain how reproducible the beneficial effects are across different samples.

paper_did: Fabricated several Nb‐silicide based alloys (ZF1, ZF2, ZF3, ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, ZF9) with controlled additions of Ge, Ti, Cr, Al, and Hf.

Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 hours using thermogravimetric analysis, GXRD, and electron microprobe techniques to examine oxide scale formation, phase evolution, and diffusion zones.

Characterized the microstructural response—including oxide scale thickness, phase composition (e.g., Nb2O5, TiNb2O7, GeO2, CrNbO4, AlNbO4), and occurrence or absence of pest oxidation and scale spallation—across different alloy formulations.
paper_reported: Alloys having only Ge (ZF1, ZF2, ZF3) suffered catastrophic pest oxidation at 800 °C, whereas those containing additional elements (Cr, Al, and Hf in ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, and ZF9) exhibited markedly improved oxidation resistance.

The oxidation kinetics varied: some alloys followed parabolic kinetics (at 800 °C) while at 1200 °C a two‐stage behavior (initial parabolic then linear) with significant scale spallation was observed.

Protective oxide phases such as Nb2O5, TiNb2O7, and GeO2 were identified, with the beneficial effects in ZF9 (which included Hf) and ZF6 highlighted through reduced scale thickness, improved phase stability, and suppression of diffusion zones.
paper_proposed: The work proposed that Ge addition can suppress pest oxidation and improve oxidation resistance in Nb‐silicide based alloys, though it noted that the synergy with Cr, Al, and Hf does not eliminate scale spallation at 1200 °C.
It suggested that further alloy design—and by extension, comparison with refractory metal High Entropy Alloys—could lead to compositions with enhanced high‐temperature oxidation performance.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Adding about 5 at.% Ge to the refractory HEA will improve high‐temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the formation of a continuous, crack‐healing GeO2–SiO2 mixed oxide scale that retards oxygen ingress.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy composed of multiple refractory elements (e.g., Nb, Ti, Mo, W, etc.) with a baseline microstructure that does not include any Ge addition.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic percent germanium into the HEA composition.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation in air at temperatures of 1200 °C for exposures up to 100 hours.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, adherent mixed oxide scale consisting of GeO2 and SiO2.
hypotheses.mechanism: Germanium, added at a critical level, will oxidize preferentially to form GeO2. When combined with Si present naturally (or as part of design) in the alloy, the resulting GeO2–SiO2 mixed scale forms a glassy, continuous layer that can quickly heal microcracks, reduce oxygen diffusion, and thereby slow further oxidation. This mechanism leverages the findings in the paper where Ge addition improved oxidation resistance through formation of protective oxides and a healing Ge-doped silica film (see PMC6804173::web::010 and PMC6804173::web::009).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated HEA, the Ge-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit a significantly lower oxidation rate (potentially by one to two orders of magnitude under the specified conditions), with the formation of a thin, continuous oxide scale and reduced scale spallation.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated HEA typically forms non-protective oxides that allow rapid oxygen ingress, leading to scale breakdown and higher weight gain under similar high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: This improvement is expected under static air at 1200 °C; however, in environments with cyclic thermal shock or in cases of very high oxygen partial pressures, the effect may be less pronounced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in oxidation rate and the scale adhesion under cyclic conditions need experimental confirmation; precise optimal Ge level might require further tuning.

paper_did: Synthesized a series of as‐cast Nb-silicide based alloys with varying compositions (e.g. Nb-18Si-5Ge, Nb-24Ti-18Si variants with additions of Ge, Cr, Al, and Hf) using arc melting.
Exposed these alloys to isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C and 1200 °C for 100 hours under controlled conditions.

Conducted detailed characterizations using thermogravimetric analysis (TG), glancing-angle X-ray diffraction (GXRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and Electron Microprobe Analysis (EPMA) to study oxidation kinetics, oxide scale composition, microstructural evolution, and diffusion zones.
paper_reported: At 800 °C, alloys with only Ge (ZF1, ZF2, ZF3) suffered catastrophic pest oxidation, whereas those with additional alloying elements (ZF4, ZF5, ZF6, ZF9) exhibited significantly improved oxidation resistance with parabolic kinetics and absence of pesting.

Different oxide phases were identified in the scales – dominant ones include Nb2O5 and TiNb2O7, with GeO2 present in all scales and additional oxides (SiO2, CrNbO4, AlNbO4, HfO2) appearing depending on the alloy composition.

The oxidation behavior at 1200 °C showed a two-stage kinetics (initial parabolic then linear) accompanied by scale spallation, and detailed differences in scale thickness, adhesion, and the presence (or absence) of an oxygen-contaminated diffusion zone were documented.

Synergistic effects of alloying additions (especially Ge together with Cr, Al, and Hf) were found to suppress pest oxidation at 800 °C, although even these did not fully prevent scale spallation at 1200 °C.
paper_proposed: Exploring alloy design strategies that combine specific alloying additions to further enhance oxidation resistance—particularly to overcome scale spallation at higher temperatures (e.g. 1200 °C).

Comparisons with refractory metal high entropy alloys (HEAs) or complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) were suggested to place the Nb-silicide based alloys in context with other advanced high-temperature materials.

paper_did: Prepared a series of WVTaTiCrx refractory high‐entropy alloy coatings (with x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) on 42-CrMo steel via laser cladding using powders of W, V, Ta, Ti, and varying Cr contents.

Mixed powders by ball milling and applied laser cladding with optimized process parameters (laser power 1.4 kW, scanning speed 8 mm/s, spot diameter 6 mm, 30–40% overlap) under an argon protective atmosphere.

Conducted detailed characterization including SEM/EDS for microstructure, XRD for phase analysis, microhardness testing along the coating cross section, high-temperature oxidation tests at 800 °C for 50 hours, and corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
paper_reported: Found that increasing Cr content refines the microstructure, promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase (Cr2Ta), and enhances the hardness, with the Cr1 sample reaching an average of approximately 627.36 HV.

Demonstrated improved high-temperature oxidation resistance with higher Cr levels, where the oxide weight gain decreased from 10.41 mg/cm² for the Cr0 sample to 5.12 mg/cm² for the Cr1 sample, and identified protective oxides (CrTaO4, TiO2, Cr2O3) via XRD.
Showed that corrosion resistance in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution improved with increasing Cr, indicated by a shift to more positive corrosion potentials and a reduction in corrosion rate.
paper_proposed: Suggested that the enhanced mechanical and oxidation properties of the developed WVTaTiCr coatings indicate potential for use in high-temperature applications such as fusion and radiation protection, addressing the shortcomings of some W‐based binary alloys.
Implied the possibility of further compositional or processing modifications to optimize performance for heat insulation and nuclear reactor applications.

paper_did: Fabricated AlxNbTiV (X = 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1) refractory high‐entropy alloys by vacuum arc melting and suction casting.
Selected Al0.8NbTiV as the optimal composition based on a balance of high yield strength, good plasticity, and low density.
Introduced minor alloying additions of Co or Ni (0.2 in the formula, i.e. Al0.8NbTiVM0.2) to promote solid‐solution strengthening.
Conducted a heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour to induce the in situ formation of sigma (σ) precipitates within the BCC matrix.
Characterized phase structure (via XRD), microstructure (via SEM and EDS), density, and compressive mechanical properties at room and elevated temperatures (700 °C and 800 °C).
paper_reported: All as‐cast alloys exhibit a single BCC solid‐solution phase, with increasing Al content leading to peak shifts (lattice contraction) and increasing yield strength.
Minor additions of Co or Ni further enhance yield strength in the as‐cast condition by solid‐solution strengthening.

Post heat‐treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour, both Co- and Ni-alloyed samples develop homogeneously distributed sigma precipitates in the BCC matrix, which further boost yield strength at room temperature but reduce plastic ductility.

paper_did: Synthesized a series of AlxNbTiV refractory high‐entropy alloys (with x = 0, 0.4, 0.8, and 1) via vacuum arc melting, suction casting, and multiple re‐melting cycles to ensure compositional homogeneity.
Selected the Al0.8NbTiV alloy for its optimal combination of high yield strength, good plasticity, and low density.
Modified the selected alloy by incorporating minor amounts (0.2 molar fraction) of Co or Ni to stimulate precipitate formation.
Applied a heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 hour to induce the formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma precipitates within the BCC matrix.
Performed microstructural (XRD, SEM/EDS) and mechanical (compression tests at room temperature, 700 °C, and 800 °C) characterizations.
paper_reported: Increasing the Al content in AlxNbTiV alloys reduces the lattice constant and significantly enhances yield strength.
The as‐cast alloys exhibit a single BCC phase, whereas the subsequent heat treatment induces the formation of sigma precipitates that are homogeneously distributed in the matrix.

Minor additions of Co or Ni further improve yield strength (via both solid‐solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening) and lead to a dual sigma precipitate population (Nb‐rich and Co/Ni‐rich) after heat treatment.

The sigma precipitates and their uniform distribution are identified as the key mechanism for improved room‐temperature and elevated-temperature (up to 700 °C) specific yield strength compared to conventional alloys such as Inconel 718.
paper_proposed: The work implies that further design optimization—specifically, controlling the formation, size, volume fraction, and distribution of secondary (sigma) phases—can be used to tailor the high‐temperature mechanical properties of light‐weight refractory HEAs.

It suggests that novel alloying strategies (beyond simple compositional tweaks) could be explored to achieve enhanced performance, although the paper itself does not investigate oxidation behavior or surface modification.

paper_did: Prepared CoCrNiAlX (X = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) medium‐entropy alloy powders by mechanical alloying using high‐purity metal powders and a mixed process control agent.
Consolidated the powders using spark‐plasma sintering (SPS) at ~1075 °C under 45 MPa for 10 minutes.
Conducted room‐temperature mechanical tests (compression, hardness) after sample preparation.
Performed high‐temperature oxidation tests at 1100 °C in air for up to 100 hours and analyzed oxide scale formation.
paper_reported: The phase evolution: at low Al (0–0.3) the alloys are single-phase face‐centered cubic (fcc) with Cr23C6 carbides and some Al2O3; at higher Al (≥0.5) a dual-phase (fcc + bcc) structure appears with increased bcc fraction alongside carbide and Al2O3 precipitation.
Mechanical properties – significant increases in yield strength (from ~1178 MPa to ~2083 MPa) and hardness (from ~429 HV to ~646 HV) with increasing Al, accompanied by a loss in plasticity.

High‐temperature oxidation resistance improved with increasing Al; formation of a protective Al2O3 scale (in combination with Cr2O3 and spinel oxides) is responsible for reducing oxidation weight gain and spallation.
paper_proposed: The study discusses how the formation of a continuous Al2O3 oxidation film is key to impeding oxygen ingress, thereby suggesting that alloy design through Al addition could be a route toward high‐temperature applications.
It implies that further development in alloy composition (such as adjusting phase balance) could pave the way for advanced oxidation‐resistant applications in high-temperature fields.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Incorporate a controlled addition of approximately 5 at% aluminum into the composition of refractory high-entropy alloys to promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale that impedes further oxygen ingress at extreme temperatures.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a MoNbTaW-based system) without significant Al content, which forms only less-protective native oxide scales.
hypotheses.intervention: Add ~5 at% aluminum uniformly during alloy production.
hypotheses.conditions: Operating at extreme temperatures around 1200 °C in air for durations up to 100 hours.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The modified alloy microstructure will facilitate the formation of an adherent, ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen with a very negative Gibbs free energy of formation for Al2O3. When present in sufficient quantity, Al atoms will preferentially oxidize to form a dense, continuous Al2O3 film that acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy. This mechanism is analogous to the improved oxidation resistance seen in Al-containing CoCrNi alloys as reported in the paper (see PMC9787501::web::017 and PMC9787501::web::016).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit significantly reduced oxidation weight gain (potentially by around 50% or more reduction relative to the untreated alloy) and improved scale adhesion under 1200 °C air exposure for 100 hours.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA, which develops less-protective oxide scales that spall under high-temperature conditions.
hypotheses.boundary: If the Al content is too low, an inadequate alumina scale may form; if too high, excessive alloying may deteriorate mechanical properties. The beneficial effect is predicted within a narrow Al addition window around 5 at%.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in weight gain reduction and long-term performance require experimental validation, as the refractory environment may influence scale growth kinetics differently compared to medium-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one standard composition and one with an additional ~5 at% Al. Expose both sets to 1200 °C in atmospheric air for 100 hours.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introduce a minor reactive element, such as about 0.5 at% yttrium (Y), into refractory high-entropy alloys to enhance the adhesion and stability of the naturally forming oxide scale at extreme temperatures.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., MoNbTaW based) that, in its untreated form, forms native oxide scales (e.g., Cr or mixed oxides) which are prone to spallation under thermal cycling.
hypotheses.intervention: Incorporate a trace addition (approximately 0.5 at%) of yttrium during alloy synthesis.
hypotheses.conditions: Expose the alloy to high temperature conditions around 1200 °C in air for 100 hours.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Yttrium segregates to the oxide scale grain boundaries, thereby modifying the scale microstructure and promoting a denser, more coherent oxide layer.
hypotheses.mechanism: Reactive element effects are well known in high-temperature oxidation where additions like Y improve oxide adhesion by modifying grain boundary diffusion and reducing stress-induced spallation. In this case, even if the alloy forms a native oxide (e.g., Cr2O3 or mixed oxides), the presence of Y will improve its adherence and integrity, thereby reducing further oxygen ingress. This approach is conceptually supported by reactive element modifications in alumina-forming austenitic steels (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::011).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The yttrium-doped alloy should exhibit a lower oxidation weight gain (with reduction details to be quantified) and improved oxide scale retention compared to the undoped alloy under identical testing conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard refractory HEA without Y addition, which shows greater oxide scale spallation and higher oxidation weight gain under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
hypotheses.boundary: The benefits rely on the yttrium content being kept very low; excessive Y may lead to the formation of undesirable intermetallic phases or precipitates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect is well documented in other high-temperature alloys, the specific quantitative improvement in refractory HEAs remains uncertain.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Implement a pre-oxidation heat treatment in a low oxygen partial pressure environment to deliberately form a thin, adherent protective oxide scale on refractory high-entropy alloys, which then enhances subsequent high-temperature oxidation resistance in service.

hypotheses.intervention: Subject the alloy surface to a pre-oxidation anneal (e.g., 900 °C for 10 hours) in an atmosphere with reduced oxygen content (e.g., 1 vol% O2 in argon) prior to actual service exposure.
hypotheses.conditions: Pre-oxidation treatment at 900 °C in 1% O2/Ar, followed by subsequent exposure to 1200 °C in atmospheric air for 100 hours during service.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The pre-oxidation process results in the formation of a uniform, dense, and thin oxide film that strongly adheres to the alloy surface.
hypotheses.mechanism: By initially exposing the alloy to a controlled environment, a deliberately grown oxide layer (which could be alumina if the alloy contains sufficient Al or another protective oxide) forms in a quasi-equilibrium state. This scale is then capable of impeding oxygen diffusion when later exposed to harsher oxidation conditions. The mechanism draws on general oxidation kinetics principles where an intact, compact oxide layer slows further oxidation (as discussed in TXT::wikipedia::Powder_metallurgy::001 and supported indirectly by the paper’s discussion on oxide stability).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The pre-oxidized alloy is expected to show a marked reduction in subsequent oxidation weight gain and improved surface integrity (less spallation) compared to an untreated alloy when exposed to 1200 °C in air.
hypotheses.baseline: The same refractory HEA without any pre-oxidation treatment, which under high-temperature exposure develops non-uniform, poorly adherent oxide scales.
hypotheses.boundary: The pre-oxidation parameters (temperature, time, and oxygen partial pressure) must be carefully optimized; too aggressive a treatment may cause thick oxide formation or scale spallation before service.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the general concept of pre-oxidation is known, the exact improvement magnitude for refractory HEAs under these specific conditions is uncertain and must be empirically determined.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s finding that the oxidation resistance at 1100 °C is associated with a denser CrTaO₄-based oxide (PMC6513993::web::009, PMC6513993::web::012) and the known benefits of forming continuous Al₂O₃ layers for passivation (TXT::wikipedia::Passivation_(chemistry)::004).
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a targeted surface enrichment strategy to promote protective Al₂O₃ formation—a strategy not explored in the paper, which primarily observes competitive oxide formation leading to a porous scale.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing the surface Al concentration via a pre-alloying treatment will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, dense Al₂O₃ layer that retards oxygen ingress and improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
fields.material_initial_state: An NV1-type refractory high-entropy alloy with a heterogeneous microstructure (Mo-rich dendrites and Cr-/Al-rich interdendritic regions) as described in PMC6513993, where the dominant external oxide is porous CrTaO₄ accompanied by dispersed Al₂O₃ and Cr₂O₃.
fields.intervention: Apply a controlled surface pre-alloying (or similar surface modification) to enrich the near‐surface region in aluminum prior to high-temperature exposure.
fields.conditions: Expose treated samples in flowing dry air at 1100 °C for 200 hours; these conditions are selected because the paper shows that at 1100 °C a denser oxide scale forms compared to 1000 °C.
fields.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent, and dense Al₂O₃ scale formed on the treated surface.
fields.mechanism: By increasing the local Al concentration at the surface, the kinetics for Al diffusion and its oxidation are enhanced. This accelerates the formation of an Al₂O₃ layer, which, due to its low oxygen permeability and high thermodynamic stability, serves as an effective barrier against further oxygen ingress. This contrasts with the porous CrTaO₄-based oxide normally forming in the untreated alloy (PMC6513993::web::009, PMC6513993::web::012).
fields.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in oxidation mass gain (potentially on the order of 30–50% lower than the untreated alloy’s ~4 mg/cm² gain over 200 hours) and the formation of a more uniform and continuous oxide scale.
fields.baseline: Untreated NV1 alloy which shows a 4.03 mg/cm² mass gain at 1100 °C over 200 hours with a predominantly porous CrTaO₄-based scale.
fields.boundary: The intervention is expected to work at temperatures where Al₂O₃ formation is kinetically accessible (e.g., near or at 1100 °C in dry air); if the Al availability or its oxidation kinetics are insufficient, the protective layer may not form.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement is uncertain due to potential complexities in multi-element diffusion and competitive oxide formation.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a small reactive element addition of yttrium (approximately 1–2 wt.%) into the Si-20Cr-20Fe slurry coating to promote the in‐situ formation of a finely dispersed, adherent yttrium-enriched oxide at the outer surface, thereby enhancing high-temperature oxygen resistance of MoNbTaTiW RHEA.

This should mitigate the rapid oxidation linked to silicon diffusion observed in the baseline coating.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxide scale growth (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide layers) compared to the untreated Si-20Cr-20Fe coating, potentially achieving a 30–50% improvement in oxidation resistance. fields.hypothesis: Applying a laser surface alloying treatment with an Al-rich overlay to create an Al-enriched surface layer will improve the high‐temperature oxygen resistance of the refractory HEA by promoting the formation of a dense, slow‐growing, adherent alumina scale.
fields.material_initial_state: An Al0.8NbTiV refractory HEA processed to form a homogeneous BCC matrix with sigma precipitates via heat treatment at 1100 °C for 1 h.
fields.intervention: Deposit a very thin (e.g., 10–20 µm) Al foil on the as-cast sample surface and subject the surface to a laser surface alloying process. This causes rapid melting and mixing of the foil with the top surface of the HEA to yield an Al-enriched layer.
fields.conditions: After the surface treatment, the sample is exposed to air at 1100 °C for 100 hours to simulate extreme-temperature service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The laser-treated surface layer, having a locally increased Al concentration, acts as a reservoir for forming a continuous and adherent Al2O3 (alumina) scale during high-temperature exposure.
fields.mechanism: The higher Al content at the surface drives the rapid nucleation and growth of a protective alumina scale that is slow growing and adherent. This scale limits oxygen ingress into the bulk, thereby significantly enhancing high-temperature oxygen resistance without altering the bulk sigma-strengthened microstructure.
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should display a markedly reduced oxidation weight gain (expected to be reduced by an order of magnitude relative to the untreated state, although the precise value is uncertain) and improved oxide scale integrity.
fields.baseline: The standard oxidation behavior of untreated Al0.8NbTiV alloy processed to develop sigma precipitates and exposed at 1100 °C in air for 100 hours.
fields.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in conditions up to ~1100 °C in air. At substantially higher temperatures or in more aggressive oxidizing environments (e.g., with added water vapor or contaminants), the protective scale may evolve differently.
fields.uncertainty: While the reactive alumina formation is well established, the quantitative improvement (e.g., precise weight gain reduction) and the robustness of the laser-induced Al enrichment under cyclic thermal exposure remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same HEA batch. Apply the laser surface alloying with an Al foil overlay on one group while keeping the other group untreated. Expose both sets to air at 1100 °C for 100 hours, then measure oxidation weight gain and examine the oxide scale morphology by SEM/EDS and XRD.
measurements: Mass change (oxidation weight gain).
Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and composition.
Surface Al concentration profiles (e.g., via EDS or SIMS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-surface-alloyed samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain or if the oxide scale is not more continuous/adherent compared to the untreated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C16
pool.builds_on: the demonstrated mechanism in the paper where Al addition promotes the formation of protective oxide films in CoCrNi alloys.
pool.what_is_new: It extends that concept to refractory high-entropy alloys, which operate under even more extreme temperature conditions and typically lack such beneficial oxidation behavior.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a controlled addition of approximately 5 at% aluminum into the composition of refractory high-entropy alloys to promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale that impedes further oxygen ingress at extreme temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a MoNbTaW-based system) without significant Al content, which forms only less-protective native oxide scales.
fields.intervention: Add ~5 at% aluminum uniformly during alloy production.
fields.conditions: Operating at extreme temperatures around 1200 °C in air for durations up to 100 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: The modified alloy microstructure will facilitate the formation of an adherent, ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface.
fields.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen with a very negative Gibbs free energy of formation for Al2O3. When present in sufficient quantity, Al atoms will preferentially oxidize to form a dense, continuous Al2O3 film that acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy. This mechanism is analogous to the improved oxidation resistance seen in Al-containing CoCrNi alloys as reported in the paper (see PMC9787501::web::017 and PMC9787501::web::016).
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit significantly reduced oxidation weight gain (potentially by around 50% or more reduction relative to the untreated alloy) and improved scale adhesion under 1200 °C air exposure for 100 hours.
fields.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA, which develops less-protective oxide scales that spall under high-temperature conditions.
fields.boundary: If the Al content is too low, an inadequate alumina scale may form; if too high, excessive alloying may deteriorate mechanical properties. The beneficial effect is predicted within a narrow Al addition window around 5 at%.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in weight gain reduction and long-term performance require experimental validation, as the refractory environment may influence scale growth kinetics differently compared to medium-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one standard composition and one with an additional ~5 at% Al. Expose both sets to 1200 °C in atmospheric air for 100 hours.
measurements: Weight gain measurements at regular intervals (e.g., every 20 hours)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis via SEM/EDS to assess oxide scale continuity and adhesion
XRD analysis to identify oxide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and does not form a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: the findings of PMC7475834 regarding the oxidation behavior of the Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating on MoNbTaTiW RHEA, while leveraging known reactive element effects from superalloy systems (TXT::wikipedia::Superalloy::030).
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a specific reactive element addition (yttrium) into the fused slurry coating formulation to improve oxide scale adhesion and reduce oxygen ingress, a mechanistic approach not explored in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a small reactive element addition of yttrium (approximately 1–2 wt.%) into the Si-20Cr-20Fe slurry coating to promote the in‐situ formation of a finely dispersed, adherent yttrium-enriched oxide at the outer surface, thereby enhancing high-temperature oxygen resistance of MoNbTaTiW RHEA.
fields.material_initial_state: MoNbTaTiW RHEA coated with the conventional fused slurry Si-20Cr-20Fe silicide coating that forms a double-layer structure (outer MSi2 and inner M5Si3) as reported in PMC7475834.
fields.intervention: Modify the slurry formulation by adding 1–2 wt.% yttrium to the Si-20Cr-20Fe mixture prior to coating deposition and thermal treatment.
fields.conditions: Static air oxidation at 1300 °C for 1 hour, which is within the extreme-temperature regime for RHEAs used in structural applications.
fields.structural_mediator: The yttrium is expected to segregate to the oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation, promoting the formation of a thin, continuous, and adherent yttrium-enriched oxide (likely a modified silicate or mixed oxide scale).
fields.mechanism: Reactive element effects (REE) such as those known from superalloy technology enhance oxide adhesion and reduce the growth rate and spallation of oxide scales. Yttrium segregates to the oxide grain boundaries and interfaces, reducing defect density and retarding oxygen diffusion into the underlying silicide and substrate layers. This should mitigate the rapid oxidation linked to silicon diffusion observed in the baseline coating.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduction in oxide scale growth (e.g., lower weight gain and thinner, more adherent oxide layers) compared to the untreated Si-20Cr-20Fe coating, potentially achieving a 30–50% improvement in oxidation resistance. The improvement is expected in the specified regime, though the exact quantitative effect has some uncertainty.
fields.baseline: The conventional Si-20Cr-20Fe coating on MoNbTaTiW RHEA, which shows multilayer oxide/silicide formation with cracks and extensive silicon diffusion upon oxidation at 1300 °C.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness is expected under static air conditions at around 1300 °C for exposures on the order of 1 hour; performance under dynamic or longer exposure conditions remains to be validated.
fields.uncertainty: The precise segregation behavior of yttrium in the complex multicomponent silicide system is uncertain; pilot experiments or thermodynamic simulations would be needed to optimize the Y content without disrupting the silicide structure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MoNbTaTiW RHEA samples: one set with the standard Si-20Cr-20Fe coating and a second set with the modified Si-20Cr-20Fe + 1–2 wt.% Y coating. Expose both sets to static air oxidation at 1300 °C for 1 hour. Characterize the coatings using weight gain measurements, XRD for oxide phase identification, and SEM/EDS to assess oxide scale thickness and morphology.
measurements: Weight gain
Oxide scale thickness
XRD phase composition
SEM/EDS microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness and weight gain, or if it does not form a continuous, adherent yttrium-enriched oxide layer compared to the standard coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C10
top3.builds_on: The findings in the paper that Ge addition aids in forming beneficial oxide phases and a healing Ge-doped silica film, extended here by ensuring sufficient Si is present to enable germanosilicate formation.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis adapts the Ge addition strategy from Nb-silicide based alloys to Si-containing refractory HEAs, ensuring the formation of a self-healing germanosilicate scale for enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance.

fields.hypothesis: Adding ~5 at.% Ge to a Si-containing refractory HEA will improve high-temperature oxygen resistance by promoting the in situ formation of a flowing, self-healing germanosilicate oxide scale.
fields.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy designed with a minimum of ~10 at.% Si (in addition to Nb, Ti, Mo, W, etc.), which in its untreated state forms relatively non-protective, brittle oxide scales at high temperatures.
fields.intervention: Introduce approximately 5 atomic percent germanium into the pre-designed Si-containing HEA composition.
fields.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 1200 °C for up to 100 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: Development of a thin, continuous, and crack-healing oxide scale composed of mixed Ge–Si oxides (germanosilicate) that adheres well to the substrate.
fields.mechanism: The added Ge oxidizes to form GeO2, which when in the presence of sufficient Si, reacts or intermixes to form a germanosilicate phase. This phase is envisaged to be glassy and have high fluidity at the operating temperature, enabling it to repair cracks or defects in the growing scale. The self-healing effect minimizes pathways for oxygen diffusion, thus retarding further oxidation. This builds on the observation that GeO2 solute in SiO2 results in a glass with high fluidity (PMC6804173::web::005).
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Ge-doped alloy is expected to show a significantly lower oxidation rate—potentially an order of magnitude reduction in oxide scale thickening and weight gain—along with a thinner, more adherent and crack-free scale.
fields.baseline: The untreated Si-containing refractory HEA typically forms brittle, porous oxide scales that spall, allowing accelerated oxygen ingress and higher weight gain.
fields.boundary: This benefit is predicted under static air conditions at 1200 °C; performance under cyclic thermal shock or in atmospheres with additional reactive species (e.g., water vapor) may vary.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in oxidation rate and the long-term stability of the germanosilicate scale under varying thermal cycles require experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one with ~5 at.% Ge added to an alloy already containing ~10 at.% Si, and a control without Ge. Expose both sets to isothermal oxidation in air at 1200 °C for 100 hours. Characterize the scale thickness, morphology, composition (using GXRD and EPMA), and measure mass gain via TG analysis.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time (thermogravimetric analysis)
Oxide scale thickness and phase identification (GXRD with glancing angles, SEM cross-sectional imaging, EPMA)
Assessment of scale integrity and crack-healing behavior (optical/SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ge-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass gain and oxide scale thickness, or if the oxide scale is not continuous and self-healing compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C16
top3.builds_on: the demonstrated mechanism in the paper where Al addition promotes the formation of protective oxide films in CoCrNi alloys.
top3.what_is_new: It extends that concept to refractory high-entropy alloys, which operate under even more extreme temperature conditions and typically lack such beneficial oxidation behavior.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporate a controlled addition of approximately 5 at% aluminum into the composition of refractory high-entropy alloys to promote the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale that impedes further oxygen ingress at extreme temperatures.
fields.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., a MoNbTaW-based system) without significant Al content, which forms only less-protective native oxide scales.
fields.intervention: Add ~5 at% aluminum uniformly during alloy production.
fields.conditions: Operating at extreme temperatures around 1200 °C in air for durations up to 100 hours.
fields.structural_mediator: The modified alloy microstructure will facilitate the formation of an adherent, ultrathin alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface.
fields.mechanism: Aluminum has a strong affinity for oxygen with a very negative Gibbs free energy of formation for Al2O3. When present in sufficient quantity, Al atoms will preferentially oxidize to form a dense, continuous Al2O3 film that acts as a barrier to further oxygen diffusion into the bulk alloy. This mechanism is analogous to the improved oxidation resistance seen in Al-containing CoCrNi alloys as reported in the paper (see PMC9787501::web::017 and PMC9787501::web::016).
fields.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to exhibit significantly reduced oxidation weight gain (potentially by around 50% or more reduction relative to the untreated alloy) and improved scale adhesion under 1200 °C air exposure for 100 hours.
fields.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA, which develops less-protective oxide scales that spall under high-temperature conditions.
fields.boundary: If the Al content is too low, an inadequate alumina scale may form; if too high, excessive alloying may deteriorate mechanical properties. The beneficial effect is predicted within a narrow Al addition window around 5 at%.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in weight gain reduction and long-term performance require experimental validation, as the refractory environment may influence scale growth kinetics differently compared to medium-entropy alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one standard composition and one with an additional ~5 at% Al. Expose both sets to 1200 °C in atmospheric air for 100 hours.
measurements: Weight gain measurements at regular intervals (e.g., every 20 hours)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis via SEM/EDS to assess oxide scale continuity and adhesion
XRD analysis to identify oxide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation weight gain and does not form a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.
